items.prompt: Compare writing a story by hand versus typing it on a computer. List TWO advantages of each method.
items.answer: Handwriting advantages: (1) You do not need electricity or a device. (2) Some people think more carefully when writing slowly by hand. Typing advantages: (1) Easy to edit — delete, retype, and move text without mess. (2) Typed writing can be shared digitally with many people at once.

steps: Think about what each method is best for. Both have strengths depending on the situation.

items.prompt: A student wants to write a class book about animals with three of her classmates. They all go home after school. Describe how they could use digital tools to work on this project together.
items.answer: They could each create or access a shared Google Doc, and each person could write about a different animal. They could see each other's sections, add comments, and make suggestions. When everyone is done, the teacher could print it or post it online as a class book.

steps: Each student writes their assigned section and can view/comment on others' work.

items.prompt: Spell-check is helpful, but it does not catch every mistake. Give an example of a mistake that spell-check would NOT catch and explain why.
items.answer: Sample: If a student types 'there' when they mean 'their,' spell-check will not catch it because 'there' is a correctly spelled word — it just is not the right word in context. Spell-check catches misspellings but not wrong word choices.

steps: Spell-check checks if a word exists in the dictionary. It cannot tell if you used the right word for the context (homophones like there/their/they're).

items.prompt: A second-grade class wants to share their personal narratives with parents and the school community. List THREE digital ways they could publish their stories.
items.answer: (1) Post them on the class or school website. (2) Create a digital slideshow with each story and share the link. (3) Email them to parents. (4) Put them in an online classroom portfolio. (5) Record the student reading the story and post the video.

steps: Digital publishing options include class websites, email, online portfolios, digital slideshows, and video recordings.

items.prompt: What is the difference between DRAFTING and PUBLISHING when using digital tools?
items.answer: Drafting is the stage where you type your ideas for the first time — your writing is rough and not finished. Publishing is the final stage where you share your completed, revised, and edited writing with an audience. Digital tools help at both stages: you draft in a word processor and publish by posting online or printing.

steps: Draft = first write; Publishing = final share.
Digital tools support both: a word processor for drafting, email/website for publishing.

items.prompt: A student types a report about dolphins. She makes a mistake in the second paragraph and wants to fix it before printing. Name TWO features of a word processor she could use to make her corrections.
items.answer: (1) She can use the Delete or Backspace key to remove the incorrect text and retype it. (2) She can use spell-check to identify any remaining misspellings. (3) She could also use the Find & Replace feature to locate a specific wrong word.

steps: Word processors offer: delete/backspace for editing, spell-check for errors, and Find & Replace for specific word changes.

items.prompt: Describe one way digital tools make it EASIER for a student to revise her writing compared to writing by hand.
items.answer: With digital tools, a student can delete a sentence and retype it without crossing anything out or using correction fluid. She can also move whole paragraphs around by cutting and pasting, which would be very difficult on paper.

steps: Digital editing advantages: delete without mess, copy/cut/paste to reorganize, no need to rewrite the whole piece.

items.prompt: A student's class is working on a shared digital writing project. She notices her partner left a section blank and forgot to finish it. What should she do?
items.answer: Sample: She could type a note or comment in the shared document asking her partner to complete the section. She could also tell her teacher so they can remind the partner. If they are allowed, she might complete the section herself and let her partner know.

steps: Collaboration tools often include commenting features. She can use these to communicate with her partner without overwriting their work.

items.prompt: How does using a word processor help a student FOCUS ON IDEAS rather than handwriting neatness?
items.answer: When typing, a student does not need to worry about how neat their letters look. They can type quickly and focus on what they want to say, knowing they can always fix spelling and formatting later. This helps ideas flow more freely.

steps: Handwriting requires attention to letter formation and neatness. Typing separates the physical act of writing from the intellectual task of composing ideas.

items.prompt: A student wants to publish her story to share with her grandparents who live far away. She cannot mail it. What digital options does she have?
items.answer: She could email the story to her grandparents, share a link to a class website where the story is posted, or send a photo of the printed copy. If her grandparents use video chat, the student could also read it to them live.

steps: Digital options for long-distance sharing: email, class website link, digital portfolio link, or video chat.

items.prompt: What does it mean to 'format' writing in a word processor? Give TWO examples of formatting options.
items.answer: Formatting means changing how the text looks on the page. Examples: (1) Making the font larger or smaller. (2) Making text bold or italic. (3) Changing the font style. (4) Adding a title or heading.

steps: Formatting affects the appearance of text. Common options include font size, bold/italic, font style, and text alignment.

items.prompt: A student says: 'I do not need to proofread my typing because spell-check will catch all my mistakes.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.answer: This is not correct. Spell-check catches misspelled words but not all errors. It will not catch: words that are spelled correctly but used in the wrong context (like 'there' vs. 'their'), missing punctuation, or grammar errors. A writer should always read through their work even after using spell-check.

steps: Spell-check has limits: it checks spelling, not meaning, grammar, or punctuation.

items.prompt: List the steps a student might follow when using digital tools to complete a writing assignment, from drafting to publishing.
items.answer: (1) Open a word processor or online document. (2) Type the first draft, focusing on ideas. (3) Read through and revise — add details, remove off-topic sentences. (4) Use spell-check to fix spelling errors. (5) Read again and make final edits. (6) Format the document (add a title, adjust font size). (7) Publish: print it, email it, or post it on a class website.

steps: The writing process with digital tools: draft, revise, spell-check, edit, format, publish.

items.prompt: Name ONE way collaborative digital writing is BETTER than writing alone, and ONE way it could be MORE CHALLENGING.
items.answer: Better: Two writers bring more ideas, catch each other's errors, and share the work so no one person carries the whole load. More challenging: Partners may disagree on ideas or write in different styles, and someone may accidentally overwrite or delete the other's work.

steps: Collaboration advantage: more ideas, shared work, peer review.
Collaboration challenge: coordination, disagreements, accidental overwriting.

items.prompt: Describe how a student could use a digital tool to share a PUBLISHED story with classmates during school. Include which tool and how classmates would access it.
items.answer: Sample: The student could post her story on the class website or in the class's Google Classroom folder. Classmates could access it by opening the class website or Google Classroom on their school tablets or computers. The teacher could also display the story on the projector screen for the whole class to read together.

steps: Sharing at school: class website, Google Classroom, shared folder, or displaying on a projector.
